metric.concurrency.assessment: Quidra's concurrency design is intentionally small and safety-first: task.all gives clean, structured (non-detachable, joined-before-return) parallelism with a bounded worker pool, deterministic per-slot result ordering, and an explicit, narrow, race-safe channel for shared mutable state (atomic.Counter) instead of general shared references. This avoids entire classes of data races and closure-capture bugs found in more permissive concurrency models. However the surface is currently narrow: no cancellation, no detached tasks, no channels/actors/futures composition, and no general managed-value (string/class/array) transfer across task boundaries -- only scalar int/float results and atomic counters. Compared to concurrency designs in Rust (fearless-concurrency ownership+Send/Sync model), Go (goroutines+channels), or even Kotlin (coroutines+structured concurrency+rich cancellation), Quidra's primitive is safer-by-restriction but much less expressive today. It is a promising, principled starting design rather than a full concurrency model.
metric.concurrency.normalization_note: Score credits the intrinsic soundness of the structured-concurrency contract (bounded, joined, capture-free, explicit shared-state channel) while reflecting the narrow expressiveness (no cancellation, no general data transfer, single primitive) relative to established languages' concurrency designs. 0-100 scale, 100 best.
raw_observations: task.all(operations) is the sole structured-concurrency primitive: it accepts fn<void>()[] for effect-only work, or (with an expected result array type) fn<int>()[] / fn<float>()[] returning results in operation-array order independent of completion order.
All operations run through a bounded worker set; the call returns only after every started operation has joined -- classic structured concurrency (no detached tasks, lexically bounded lifetime).

Shared mutable state requires the explicit atomic.Counter type via task.all(operations, counter), which passes an independently owned handle into each operation; this is the only writable cross-task-sharing mechanism -- there is no implicit capture or ordinary managed-value sharing across tasks.
Function values used as task bodies are capture-free, which removes a large class of data-race bugs common to closures capturing mutable state in other languages.

Explicitly documented current limitations: cancellation, detached task lifetime, and broader managed-value result transfer (beyond int[]/float[]) are NOT yet implemented -- 'remain development areas' per the Implementation scope section.

Managed ownership bookkeeping (retain/release) is documented as thread-local in the current runtime, and the spec explicitly states cross-thread sharing of managed values is not currently exposed, with a note that this assumption 'must be revisited explicitly' if a future concurrency model introduces such sharing -- i.e. only scalar results and atomic-cell sharing are safely concurrent today; general managed objects (strings, classes, arrays) are not passed across task boundaries.

GPU work is asynchronous by default with an explicit synchronization model (gpu.sync, sync=true args on time.now/time.since) that composes with but is architecturally separate from the CPU task.all structured-concurrency model.
metric.concurrency.source: /quidra-benchmark/repo/docs/spec/language.md, sections 'Structured concurrency' and preceding paragraph on atomic.Counter/ownership

metric.ffi_interoperability_design.assessment: Quidra's FFI design is deliberately minimal and safety-first: a clean scalar/void ABI, explicit borrowed-span passing for text/binary with byte-aligned length metadata (avoiding both copies and unsafe raw pointer exposure), explicit ABI-extension rules matching C conventions, no implicit linking/loading, and no silent error swallowing. This is a well-thought-out, principled interop boundary, but it intentionally omits struct/aggregate passage, generics, arrays, and managed-value transfer across the boundary, which more mature FFI systems (e.g. Rust's #[repr(C)] struct support, Zig's native C struct ABI, C++'s direct C compatibility) support more broadly. It reflects strong design intent but a narrower practical surface than languages built around large-scale C interop.
metric.ffi_interoperability_design.normalization_note: Score reflects strength of documented design principles (borrow safety, no hidden allocation, explicit failure handling, no implicit linking) offset by narrow surface area (scalars + borrowed span buffers only; no structs/arrays/generics across the boundary). 0-100 scale, 100 best.
raw_observations: Quidra exposes a deliberately narrow C ABI boundary via top-level extern declarations binding a Quidra function name to an explicit C symbol, e.g. extern int c_abs(int value) = "llabs".

Only ABI-stable by-value scalars (fixed-width int/uint, int/int64, float32, float/float64, bool) and void are permitted as parameters/results; no arrays, tensors, neural values, unions, classes, generics, default args, or scalar references may cross the boundary.

Managed buffers cross only via explicit call-scoped storage borrows: const string &, const bin &, bin &, each lowered to a (pointer, uint64 length) pair at the ABI boundary; no implicit NUL-termination assumption, no encoding conversion, pointers may not be retained after the call.
Mutable string & is disallowed across the boundary specifically to preserve the UTF-8 invariant against foreign mutation -- a safety-motivated interop restriction.

Capture-free Quidra function values may cross as C callback pointers, restricted to a narrower scalar set (excludes 8/16-bit ints and bool) precisely to avoid platform-dependent ABI-extension inconsistencies; callbacks carry no capture environment so there is no hidden allocation or captured-object lifetime issue.
Integer ABI extension (signext/zeroext) is explicit and specified per width, matching platform C ABI conventions on both declaration and call sites.
Foreign failure is never inferred from errno/null/convention: callers must expose an explicit scalar status and handle it in Quidra -- avoids silent foreign-error propagation.

Symbol binding is explicit and collision-checked: reserved runtime/mangling namespaces (main, n_*, quidra_*, __quidra_*) cannot be rebound; duplicate extern aliases for the same C symbol are rejected at check time.

Linking of foreign objects/archives/shared libraries is explicit only (repeatable --link FILE on quidra build/run/debug); no implicit library search, no build-time network access, and the core declaration performs no library loading or foreign initialization code.
External calls are treated as potentially effectful by the REPL so accumulated-source replay never silently re-executes them.
